**LEGAL & INSTITUTIONAL ACCOUNTABILITY STRATEGY**

**Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough**

*Client working note, prepared for review by instructed solicitors and counsel — August 2026* 

*Version 0.3*

**This note is not legal advice. It replaces the earlier working notes following a further review focused on legal precision. It is prepared for you to hand to instructed solicitors and counsel, who should treat every recommendation as provisional pending their own review of the full papers. No solicitor-client relationship is created by it.**

# Part I — Executive Summary

This note does not claim to have identified a route through which the historic events can now be litigated. It sets out a set of potentially viable routes. Each has a different claimant, a different defendant, a different cause of action, a different limitation regime, a different evidential burden, and a different procedure, and several remain entirely conditional on counsel's opinion before any step is taken. That is a less dramatic proposition than an earlier draft of this note advanced, but it is a more defensible one, and it is considerably harder for an opposing party to dismiss as speculative.

The underlying architecture still holds: determine the property/title question first; treat institutional accountability as a separate and harder question; gather evidence across both; and track limitation on a claim-by-claim, defendant-by-defendant basis rather than as a single family-history proposition. What has changed in this edition is the precision with which each of those pieces is described, and in several places that precision cuts against propositions in the earlier draft that were stated too broadly.

# Part II — The Four Separate Questions

Everything in this note answers one of four distinct questions. Keeping them separate is the single most important discipline in the whole strategy, because conflating them is where earlier drafts (and many family-history narratives generally) go wrong.

1. What is the true title to the House Plot? — a property law question, answered from conveyances, plans, and the registration history.

2. What exactly did the 1987 Court of Appeal determine, and what did it leave open? — a question of precedent and estoppel, answered from the judgment itself.

3. What historic institutional acts or omissions are evidenced? — a question of fact, answered from surviving and reconstructed records.

4. What present legal remedies, if any, remain available, against whom, and within what time limit? — a question of live causes of action and limitation, answered by counsel.

A missing record answers question 3\. It does not, by itself, answer question 4\. A finding that the 1987 judgment did not decide root-of-title answers question 2\. It does not, by itself, establish the answer to question 1\. Keep these apart throughout.

# Part III — Evidence Architecture

The CADW critique demonstrated the practical utility of a disciplined records-lifecycle framework on the evidence available in that instance. That is a narrower claim than saying the methodology has been validated in general, and it is the more accurate one to carry forward.

| Category | Definition |
| :---- | :---- |
| Established / presently evidenced | Supported by an identified, contemporaneous source that can be independently checked. |
| Reasonable inference | A conclusion reasonably drawn from identified evidence, but not itself independently established. |
| Not presently established | The proposition cannot presently be proved from the available material — but further evidence may yet exist. This is deliberately not the same as saying the proposition is false or impossible to prove. |

A common evidential framework should be applied consistently across every institution, but not an identical audit — a Land Registry first-registration file, a police operational file, a planning file, and a heritage inspection file are different documentary ecosystems, each with its own statutory retention regime. Standardise the analytical method; identify the institution-specific record regime separately for each body.

## The evidential chain from a missing record

Earlier drafts moved too quickly from a missing record to institutional failure. The defensible chain has more steps, and each should be worked through before a conclusion is drawn: the record was expected to exist — there is evidence it once existed — it is presently absent — the institution's explanation for that absence — the retention regime actually applicable to it — whether the search and any disposal were lawful and reasonable — the evidential significance of the gap — and, only then, whatever inference is properly available. Courts distinguish routine destruction, innocent loss, and deliberate destruction, and missing records do not reverse the burden of proof. An adverse inference, if sought, needs the precise inference identified and a proper evidential foundation — it is not generated automatically by an institution's inability to produce a file.

## Four distinct routes to information — do not conflate them

| Route | What it actually gets you |
| :---- | :---- |
| FOI / Environmental Information Regulations | Recorded information already held by a public authority. It does not compel an authority to create a new answer to a question it was not already holding recorded. Frame requests around recorded things: retention schedules, disposal policies, destruction certificates, transfer and accession records, catalogues, search logs, file indexes, and any recorded communications with archive institutions or recorded reasons for destruction or transfer — not open questions like “why did you lose the file?”, which can simply be met with “we do not know.” |
| Subject Access Request (GDPR / DPA 2018\) | The living requester's own personal data only. A SAR cannot be used to obtain a deceased relative's records, and should not be presented to the family as a family-archive tool. It is useful only where a named living family member's own personal data is held by the institution. |
| Archival / statutory access | Historical records held by archives (Glamorgan Archives, National Archives, RCAHMW) under their own access rules — not a data-protection or freedom-of-information mechanism. |
| Disclosure in proceedings | Documents relevant to live litigation, obtained once a claim is issued or through pre-action disclosure applications — not available before a genuine dispute exists. |

# Part IV — The 1987 Judgment: What It Decided and What It Left Open

This is the section most likely to be tested by an opponent, and it needs to be exact rather than persuasive.

The Court of Appeal in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler \[1987\] EWCA Civ 2 did not simply find that Mrs Buckler “accepted” the October 1974 letters in the ordinary contractual sense. Dillon LJ recognised that it would be artificial to treat the position in strict contractual terms — there was no consideration, and no clear moment of acceptance. What the Court held was narrower and more specific: because Mrs Buckler received the letters and did not repudiate them, her occupation thereafter proceeded on the basis of a rent-free licence, and consequently ceased to be adverse for limitation purposes from that point.

The judgment also records, as part of the background to that finding, that BP Properties Ltd held the paper title to the farm and had been registered proprietors since first registration in November 1982\. That is a recorded fact in the judgment, not a matter left open. So the correct position is not that the 1987 case has nothing to do with title — it plainly does, and a defendant will rely on those title-related premises. The correct and defensible position is narrower still: the judgment contains title-related premises on which a defendant will rely, but it does not appear to have adjudicated the contested root-of-title question now proposed — namely, whether the House Plot itself was ever part of the proprietary chain conveyed through WGR to BP, as distinct from BP's status as registered proprietor of the farm generally.

## Estoppel / abuse-of-process attack map

Counsel should complete a table in this form before drafting, testing each proposition the defendant is likely to rely on from 1987:

| 1987 proposition | Actually litigated? | Necessary to the decision? | Does the present claim depend on contradicting it? |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| BP held “paper title” to the farm | Recorded as background fact | Not directly — background only | Potentially, if the present claim challenges the scope of that paper title |
| BP was registered proprietor from Nov 1982 | Yes, recorded fact | Relevant to limitation reasoning | No — registration date is not disputed; its scope is |
| House Plot lay within BP's registered title | Assumed rather than contested | Relevant factual premise, not a contested issue | Potentially — this is the crux of the present claim |
| The 1974 letters created a licence, ending adverse possession | Yes, the central holding | Yes — this was the ratio | No — the present claim does not need to disturb this finding |
| The root of title ran validly from WGR through to BP | Not contested or examined on the appeal | Not necessary to the adverse-possession finding | Yes — this is exactly what the present claim asks the court to determine |

This table, completed properly by counsel with the full 1987 bundle, is what will actually determine whether the root-of-title claim survives a strike-out application — not a general assertion that 1987 “didn't decide ownership.”

# Part V — Title / Rectification Track

The claim is not reducible to a single question. It requires a sequence to be established, and a gap at any point in the sequence is a gap in the claim, not a detail to be assumed away.

1. What land was legally conveyed by the 1938 WGR conveyance, on its own plan and description?

2. What land was legally conveyed by the 1975 conveyance into the BP chain, on its own plan and description?

3. What land was actually presented for first registration in 1982, and on what application documents?

4. What land was actually registered under WA231076 as a result?

5. If there is a discrepancy between (2)/(3) and (4), does that discrepancy amount to a mistake in the register within the meaning of Schedule 4 LRA 2002 — as distinct from merely a mistake in an earlier deed, which is not the same thing?

6. If a Schedule 4 mistake is established, what alteration or rectification should follow?

7. What consequences, if any, follow from the 1987 judgment and any later transactions affecting the title?

Step 5 deserves particular attention: HM Land Registry's own guidance is clear that an error in an underlying deed is not automatically a mistake in the register. The 1975 conveyance's apparent exclusion of the farmhouse, garden and curtilage is important evidence, but the claim needs to trace that exclusion (or its absence) through to what was actually presented and registered in 1982, rather than jumping directly from “1975 excluded the house” to “therefore 1982 was wrong.”

## No burden-shifting claim

An earlier version of this note stated that putting the registered proprietor to proof of its title-entry instrument “shifts the burden” onto it. That should not be repeated. The Claimants still carry the burden of establishing, from the surviving conveyancing and registration evidence, why the inclusion of the House Plot was mistaken. Requiring disclosure of the proprietor's instruments is a legitimate and important evidential step, but it is a disclosure request, not a transfer of the legal burden of proof, and should be pleaded as such.

## The possession problem — a gate, not a footnote

Schedule 4 LRA 2002 does not operate simply as “register wrong, court fixes it.” Where the current registered proprietor is in possession of the land, rectification against that proprietor is restricted unless the proprietor caused or substantially contributed to the mistake by fraud or lack of proper care, or it would for some other reason be unjust not to rectify. This makes the following a threshold inquiry, not background colour:

* Who is the current registered proprietor of WA231076?

* Who is physically in possession of the land, and on what basis?

* What presently stands on the site, and who owns or controls it?

* Has the title been transferred, charged, subdivided, or otherwise dealt with since 1982?

Note also that a Land Registry title plan generally shows only the general boundaries of a registered title, not its exact legal boundary — the red edging on the plan is not itself definitive, and the legal extent depends on the underlying conveyances and associated evidence. That makes the 1975 conveyance plan exercise in Part IV more important, not less.

# Part VI — Limitation and Section 32

## Ordinary tort limitation

The ordinary limitation period for a tort claim is six years from accrual of the cause of action. There is no general “discoverability” alternative available across the board — that only applies under specific statutory extensions for particular categories of claim (for example, certain latent-damage negligence claims). The correct approach for this note is to state the ordinary six-year rule and flag that counsel must identify whether any specific statutory extension applies to the particular duty and damage pleaded against each institution, rather than presenting “accrual or discoverability” as a general choice.

## Section 32 — a defendant-by-defendant evidential test, not a family-history proposition

Canada Square Operations Ltd v Potter \[2023\] UKSC 41 confirmed that section 32(1)(b) postpones limitation only where a fact relevant to the right of action has been deliberately — intentionally — concealed by the defendant. Recklessness is not enough, and no separate duty of disclosure needs to be shown. But section 32 concerns concealment by the defendant to the particular claim (or specified persons through whom that defendant claims). Mary Williams' account of the blanket-box papers is important evidence, but it does not automatically postpone limitation against CADW, the police, the council, or the Land Registry. For each of those, the question is whether there is evidence connecting concealment to that specific defendant and to a fact relevant to that specific cause of action. Treat section 32 as a claim-by-claim test to be built and evidenced separately, not as a single argument that unlocks every institutional claim at once.

## Human Rights Act — a specialist, conditional track, not the strongest route

This is the most legally exposed part of the earlier draft and needs to be recast. The events of December 1988 occurred twelve years before the Human Rights Act came into domestic force on 2 October 2000\. The House of Lords held in In re McKerr \[2004\] UKHL 12 that the Act is not retrospective, and that the fact that a historic event has continuing consequences does not by itself convert the original event into a domestic HRA breach. Section 7(5) HRA provides one year from the date of the act complained of, extendable at the court's discretion where equitable — not a general “date of knowledge” rule of the kind that applies in negligence.

HRA should therefore be described as a specialist conditional track, viable only if counsel can identify: (1) an act or omission occurring on or after 2 October 2000 capable of engaging the Convention; (2) a genuinely continuing Convention obligation, on the McKerr analysis, rather than merely continuing consequences of a pre-2000 event; (3) an identifiable, presently challengeable act by a public authority; (4) victim standing; and (5) a viable remedy notwithstanding the one-year limitation. Article 3 should not be pleaded unless the evidence describes conduct capable of meeting its exceptionally high threshold — including it without a specific evidential foundation makes the whole document look more expansive than the facts support.

## Ancillary causes of action

Unjust enrichment should not be presented, as an earlier draft did, as though continued retention of disputed land automatically refreshes a rolling six-year limitation period. A defect in title is not automatically an unjust-enrichment claim. This and any other ancillary doctrine (proprietary estoppel, for example) should sit in a holding category — potential ancillary causes of action, to be identified by counsel only if a specific unjust factor, enrichment, and at-the-expense-of relationship can actually be shown — rather than being presented as an active head of claim in the main strategy.

# Part VII — Institutional Accountability Tracks

Two corrections apply across this whole Part: first, “CADW” and “South Wales Police” are institutional labels, not necessarily the correct legal defendants; and second, continuity of an institution's name since 1988 does not by itself establish that today's body carries yesterday's liability.

| Institution (as commonly named) | Correct legal-identity question for counsel | Claim vehicle (subject to Part VI thresholds) | Status / priority |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| CADW | Cadw is understood to have no separate legal personality of its own and to sit within Welsh Government; the correct defendant is likely the Welsh Ministers (or, for the 1988 act, the Secretary of State for Wales / Welsh Office as it then was). Counsel must confirm the statutory decision-maker and any successor-liability route before pleading. | Negligence / misfeasance (subject to Part IV/VI thresholds); HRA only if the Part VI conditions are met | Most advanced evidential track — forensic critique v5.0.0 complete; legal identity of the defendant not yet confirmed |
| South Wales Police | Civil proceedings against a police force are conventionally brought against the Chief Constable of South Wales Police (or the relevant office-holder in 1988), not the force as an unincorporated body. Confirm this before any letter before claim is drafted. | Misconduct; negligence (subject to duty-of-care threshold) | Not started — high evidential value given Mary Williams' account, but defendant identity must be confirmed first |
| Vale of Glamorgan Council | The present Vale of Glamorgan Council dates from the 1996 local government reorganisation. Wales operated a two-tier county/district structure in 1988\. Counsel must identify which authority (county or district) actually exercised the relevant planning or Building Preservation Notice function in December 1988, and the statutory mechanism by which any liability or function passed to the present council. | Negligence; breach of statutory duty (subject to duty-of-care threshold) | Not started — begin the predecessor/successor analysis before any complaint or FOI is sent |
| Building Preservation Notice question | The current BPN framework (and its Welsh replacement, the Historic Environment (Wales) Act 2023\) post-dates 1988\. Before treating the absence of a BPN as a failure, identify what statutory power existed in December 1988, who held it, who could initiate it, and what role Cadw, the Welsh Office, and the local planning authority each actually had. | Feeds into the council and CADW tracks once resolved | Research gate — do not assert a BPN failure as fact until this is verified |
| Land Registry / Chief Land Registrar | Already correctly named. Second Defendant in the anchor claim. | Rectification (LRA 2002 Sch 4, subject to the possession restriction in Part V); Sch 8 indemnity if rectification causes loss | Already pleaded — no separate track needed unless a distinct registration-process failure is shown |
| Western Ground Rents Ltd (or successor) | Not automatically a contribution or third-party defendant — contribution is a mechanism between parties liable for the same damage and has its own limitation regime. WGR is better treated, for now, as a historical proprietary-chain evidence source and a possible party subject to separate corporate-existence and limitation analysis. | To be determined once corporate status is established | Not started — confirm whether WGR still exists as a legal entity before assigning it any claim vehicle |
| HMCTS / National Archives, RCAHMW, GGAT/Heneb | Evidential only — not prospective defendants. | None — archival/FOI requests only | Not started (HMCTS/NA, GGAT/Heneb); partially covered (RCAHMW) |
| Judiciary / the courts (1955 order; 1987 CA judgment) | Not a prospective defendant. | None — addressed only through the estoppel analysis in Part IV | Not a claim track |
| Central government / EU bodies | Requires precise identification of a specific department or agency and a viable cause of action before any track can start. | Uncertain — likely political rather than private law | Hold — counsel to advise on justiciability and standing |

# Part VIII — Information, Records and Preservation

Use the four routes in Part III deliberately rather than interchangeably: FOI/EIR for institutional recorded information; SAR strictly for a living family member's own personal data; archival access for historical material; and court disclosure once proceedings are genuinely live.

On preservation: an earlier draft stated that, once litigation is in contemplation, “nothing can lawfully be destroyed.” That overstates the position. The defensible formulation is that preservation notices should be issued identifying the specific material relevant to reasonably contemplated proceedings, and requesting suspension of routine disposal of potentially relevant records pending clarification of the dispute and the applicable retention obligations — not an assertion that all ordinary disposal processes become unlawful in every circumstance the moment a claim is contemplated.

# Part IX — Procedure and Pre-Action Strategy

There is no single universal pre-action sequence that applies to every institution and every cause of action. An earlier draft proposed one fixed six-step sequence (complaint → FOI → SAR → ombudsman → letter before claim → proceedings) for every party. That should be replaced with a route-specific approach, because judicial review in particular cannot safely be made to wait behind the others.

| Route | What applies |
| :---- | :---- |
| Evidence route | FOI / EIR / archive / data-protection requests, used as set out in Parts III and VIII, run at any time and not conditional on the other routes. |
| Complaint / regulatory route | Used only where the relevant mechanism (internal complaint, Public Services Ombudsman for Wales, IOPC, ICO) can produce a useful determination, or is itself a genuine prerequisite to a later step. It is a parallel accountability and evidential mechanism, not a litigation stage in its own right. |
| Private law route (negligence, misfeasance, contract, property) | Follow the relevant Civil Procedure Rules Pre-Action Protocol; send preservation and disclosure correspondence; issue a letter before claim once the position is sufficiently developed. |
| Judicial review route | Take specialist advice immediately if any live public-law decision is to be challenged. Judicial review claims must be filed promptly and in any event generally within three months of the decision — the general pre-action protocol does not extend that deadline, and this timetable must not be allowed to run behind information-gathering on other routes. |

**Two points apply to every route and should be stated prominently rather than left implicit:**

**FOI does not stop limitation running. SAR does not stop limitation running. An ombudsman or regulator complaint does not stop limitation running. A preservation letter does not stop limitation running. Only issuing a claim form (or, in judicial review, filing promptly within the applicable time limit) protects the position on the clock.**

The Public Services Ombudsman for Wales may decline to investigate where an adequate court remedy exists, and generally expects complaints within a year of the complainant becoming aware of the matter. An IOPC complaint can still be made after twelve months, but the complainant must explain the delay and there is no guarantee it will be investigated. Both are useful, genuinely independent routes to evidence and findings — neither is a limitation-preservation mechanism, and neither should be scheduled as though it were.

## Protective claim forms — a caveat, not a routine tool

Where a limitation deadline is genuinely at risk, counsel should determine whether a claim must be issued protectively, with any application for a stay pending pre-action protocol compliance made on a properly reasoned basis. This is a discretionary court process, not an entitlement, and must not be relied upon as though it automatically extends limitation or the judicial review promptness requirement.

# Part X — Costs and Sustainability

A multi-year campaign against several public bodies and a private registered proprietor is expensive in money, time, and emotional load. Treat that as a hard constraint on pace, not a line in a risk register.

* Investigate conditional fee agreements (CFAs) or damages-based agreements (DBAs), and after-the-event (ATE) insurance, before any institutional claim is issued.

* Consider protective costs orders for any claim genuinely of general public importance.

* Sequencing itself controls cost — do not run every front at once.

* Set the pace by the family's capacity to sustain the process, not only by procedural deadlines.

# Part XI — Risk Register

| Risk | Where it bites | Mitigation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1987 judgment's title-related premises are mischaracterised or overstated | Anchor claim | Use the estoppel attack map in Part IV; obtain the full 1987 bundle before drafting |
| Section 32 argument treated as a blanket proposition rather than defendant-specific | All tort claims relying on concealment | Build and evidence the concealment case separately against each defendant, per Part VI |
| HRA claim pleaded as though it converts a 1988 event into a live breach | Any HRA track | Apply the McKerr / s.7(5) analysis in Part VI before pleading; treat as a specialist conditional track |
| Duty of care or misfeasance threshold not met | CADW / council / police claims | Obtain counsel's threshold opinion before drafting; do not plead speculatively |
| Wrong legal defendant named (institutional label used instead of correct legal person) | CADW, police, council tracks | Resolve the legal-identity questions in Part VII before any letter before claim is sent |
| Judicial review promptness missed because information-gathering was allowed to run first | Any live public-law decision | Treat JR as its own route with its own three-month clock, per Part IX — never subordinate it to FOI/SAR/complaint timing |
| Missing records treated as proof of liability rather than as an evidential question | All institutional tracks | Apply the evidential chain in Part III; do not skip from absence to failure to liability |
| Costs exposure across multiple fronts | Institutional claims phase | Sequencing; protective costs orders; CFA/DBA and ATE insurance investigated early |

# Part XII — Issue-Readiness Gates

Before any claim is issued against any defendant, the following should be capable of a clear answer. This is deliberately the last substantive section: it turns the rest of this note from a campaign plan into a set of questions counsel can actually sign off against.

| Gate | Question |
| :---- | :---- |
| Title | Is there sufficient evidence that the House Plot was excluded from the relevant proprietary chain? |
| 1987 | Has counsel completed the estoppel attack map and confirmed precisely what was and was not adjudicated? |
| Standing | Are the correct persons entitled to sue identified and, if numerous, is a representation order needed? |
| Defendant | Is the correct legal person identified — not just the institutional label? |
| Possession | Who is presently in possession of the registered land, and does the Schedule 4 possession restriction apply? |
| Registration | Is Schedule 4 rectification actually the correct procedural mechanism on the facts established? |
| Limitation | What is the exact limitation period and trigger date for this specific cause of action against this specific defendant? |
| Section 32 | Is there defendant-specific evidence of deliberate concealment, tested against the Canada Square standard? |
| Public body | What exact statutory function or duty existed at the relevant historical date, and who held it? |
| Evidence | What critical missing document remains genuinely necessary before this claim can be pleaded? |
| Procedure | Is there a mandatory or relevant pre-action protocol, or a judicial review promptness clock, that governs this route? |
| Costs | Is the family realistically able to sustain this specific claim to conclusion? |

# Part XIII — Immediate Actions

| Priority | Action | Responsible | Deadline |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Identify the current registered proprietor of WA231076 from the Land Registry, and confirm who is in physical possession of the land | Solicitors | Week 1 |
| 2 | Confirm the correct legal defendant for the CADW track (Welsh Ministers / Welsh Office successor) and the police track (Chief Constable of South Wales Police) | Solicitors | Week 2 |
| 3 | Identify which local authority exercised the relevant planning/BPN function in December 1988, under the two-tier structure then in place, and how any liability passed to the present Vale of Glamorgan Council | Solicitors | Month 1 |
| 4 | Verify the December 1988 statutory framework for Building Preservation Notices before treating their absence as a failure | Solicitors / counsel | Month 1 |
| 5 | Commission the 1877 instrument search at Glamorgan Archives (D/D BUTE) and the National Archives | Solicitors / agent | Month 1 |
| 6 | Send preservation letters (in the terms set out in Part VIII, not an absolute non-destruction claim) to all prospective defendants | Solicitors | Week 1 |
| 7 | Instruct counsel for a written opinion completing the estoppel attack map (Part IV) and the Issue-Readiness Gates (Part XII) for the title claim specifically | Solicitors | Month 1 |
| 8 | Instruct counsel for a written opinion on section 32 (defendant-by-defendant) and on whether any HRA track can meet the Part VI conditions | Solicitors | Month 1 |
| 9 | Confirm whether any live public-law decision exists that triggers a judicial review promptness clock, and if so take specialist JR advice immediately, in parallel with everything else | Solicitors | Immediately |
| 10 | Investigate CFA/DBA and ATE insurance options before any institutional claim is issued | Solicitors | Month 1 |

**The decisive next step is not further drafting. It is counsel's written opinion on the Part IV estoppel analysis and the Part VI limitation position, tested against the Issue-Readiness Gates in Part XII. Everything else in this note remains provisional until that opinion is in hand.**

*This document does not constitute legal advice and should be reviewed, corrected, and adopted or discarded section by section by solicitors and counsel instructed on the full papers.*

The Court of Appeal in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler \[1987\] EWCA Civ 2 did not simply find that Mrs Buckler “accepted” the October 1974 letters in the ordinary contractual sense. Dillon LJ recognised that it would be artificial to treat the position in strict contractual terms — there was no consideration, and no clear moment of acceptance. What the Court held was narrower and more specific: because Mrs Buckler received the letters and did not repudiate them, her occupation thereafter proceeded on the basis of a rent-free licence, and consequently ceased to be adverse for limitation purposes from that point.

The judgment also records, as part of the background to that finding, that BP Properties Ltd held the paper title to the farm and had been registered proprietors since first registration in November 1982\. That is a recorded fact in the judgment, not a matter left open. So the correct position is not that the 1987 case has nothing to do with title — it plainly does, and a defendant will rely on those title-related premises. The correct and defensible position is narrower still: the judgment contains title-related premises on which a defendant will rely, but it does not appear to have adjudicated the contested root-of-title question now proposed — namely, whether the House Plot itself was ever part of the proprietary chain conveyed through WGR to BP, as distinct from BP's status as registered proprietor of the farm generally.

## Estoppel / abuse-of-process attack map

Counsel should complete a table in this form before drafting, testing each proposition the defendant is likely to rely on from 1987:

| 1987 proposition | Actually litigated? | Necessary to the decision? | Does the present claim depend on contradicting it? |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| BP held “paper title” to the farm | Recorded as background fact | Not directly — background only | Potentially, if the present claim challenges the scope of that paper title |
| BP was registered proprietor from Nov 1982 | Yes, recorded fact | Relevant to limitation reasoning | No — registration date is not disputed; its scope is |
| House Plot lay within BP's registered title | Assumed rather than contested | Relevant factual premise, not a contested issue | Potentially — this is the crux of the present claim |
| The 1974 letters created a licence, ending adverse possession | Yes, the central holding | Yes — this was the ratio | No — the present claim does not need to disturb this finding |
| The root of title ran validly from WGR through to BP | Not contested or examined on the appeal | Not necessary to the adverse-possession finding | Yes — this is exactly what the present claim asks the court to determine |

This table, completed properly by counsel with the full 1987 bundle, is what will actually determine whether the root-of-title claim survives a strike-out application — not a general assertion that 1987 “didn't decide ownership.”

# Part V — Title / Rectification Track

The claim is not reducible to a single question. It requires a sequence to be established, and a gap at any point in the sequence is a gap in the claim, not a detail to be assumed away.

1. What land was legally conveyed by the 1938 WGR conveyance, on its own plan and description?

2. What land was legally conveyed by the 1975 conveyance into the BP chain, on its own plan and description?

3. What land was actually presented for first registration in 1982, and on what application documents?

4. What land was actually registered under WA231076 as a result?

5. If there is a discrepancy between (2)/(3) and (4), does that discrepancy amount to a mistake in the register within the meaning of Schedule 4 LRA 2002 — as distinct from merely a mistake in an earlier deed, which is not the same thing?

6. If a Schedule 4 mistake is established, what alteration or rectification should follow?

7. What consequences, if any, follow from the 1987 judgment and any later transactions affecting the title?

Step 5 deserves particular attention: HM Land Registry's own guidance is clear that an error in an underlying deed is not automatically a mistake in the register. The 1975 conveyance's apparent exclusion of the farmhouse, garden and curtilage is important evidence, but the claim needs to trace that exclusion (or its absence) through to what was actually presented and registered in 1982, rather than jumping directly from “1975 excluded the house” to “therefore 1982 was wrong.”

## No burden-shifting claim

An earlier version of this note stated that putting the registered proprietor to proof of its title-entry instrument “shifts the burden” onto it. That should not be repeated. The Claimants still carry the burden of establishing, from the surviving conveyancing and registration evidence, why the inclusion of the House Plot was mistaken. Requiring disclosure of the proprietor's instruments is a legitimate and important evidential step, but it is a disclosure request, not a transfer of the legal burden of proof, and should be pleaded as such.

## The possession problem — a gate, not a footnote

Schedule 4 LRA 2002 does not operate simply as “register wrong, court fixes it.” Where the current registered proprietor is in possession of the land, rectification against that proprietor is restricted unless the proprietor caused or substantially contributed to the mistake by fraud or lack of proper care, or it would for some other reason be unjust not to rectify. This makes the following a threshold inquiry, not background colour:

* Who is the current registered proprietor of WA231076?

* Who is physically in possession of the land, and on what basis?

* What presently stands on the site, and who owns or controls it?

* Has the title been transferred, charged, subdivided, or otherwise dealt with since 1982?

Note also that a Land Registry title plan generally shows only the general boundaries of a registered title, not its exact legal boundary — the red edging on the plan is not itself definitive, and the legal extent depends on the underlying conveyances and associated evidence. That makes the 1975 conveyance plan exercise in Part IV more important, not less.

# Part VI — Limitation and Section 32

## Ordinary tort limitation

The ordinary limitation period for a tort claim is six years from accrual of the cause of action. There is no general “discoverability” alternative available across the board — that only applies under specific statutory extensions for particular categories of claim (for example, certain latent-damage negligence claims). The correct approach for this note is to state the ordinary six-year rule and flag that counsel must identify whether any specific statutory extension applies to the particular duty and damage pleaded against each institution, rather than presenting “accrual or discoverability” as a general choice.

## Section 32 — a defendant-by-defendant evidential test, not a family-history proposition

Canada Square Operations Ltd v Potter \[2023\] UKSC 41 confirmed that section 32(1)(b) postpones limitation only where a fact relevant to the right of action has been deliberately — intentionally — concealed by the defendant. Recklessness is not enough, and no separate duty of disclosure needs to be shown. But section 32 concerns concealment by the defendant to the particular claim (or specified persons through whom that defendant claims). Mary Williams' account of the blanket-box papers is important evidence, but it does not automatically postpone limitation against CADW, the police, the council, or the Land Registry. For each of those, the question is whether there is evidence connecting concealment to that specific defendant and to a fact relevant to that specific cause of action. Treat section 32 as a claim-by-claim test to be built and evidenced separately, not as a single argument that unlocks every institutional claim at once.

## Human Rights Act — a specialist, conditional track, not the strongest route

This is the most legally exposed part of the earlier draft and needs to be recast. The events of December 1988 occurred twelve years before the Human Rights Act came into domestic force on 2 October 2000\. The House of Lords held in In re McKerr \[2004\] UKHL 12 that the Act is not retrospective, and that the fact that a historic event has continuing consequences does not by itself convert the original event into a domestic HRA breach. Section 7(5) HRA provides one year from the date of the act complained of, extendable at the court's discretion where equitable — not a general “date of knowledge” rule of the kind that applies in negligence.

HRA should therefore be described as a specialist conditional track, viable only if counsel can identify: (1) an act or omission occurring on or after 2 October 2000 capable of engaging the Convention; (2) a genuinely continuing Convention obligation, on the McKerr analysis, rather than merely continuing consequences of a pre-2000 event; (3) an identifiable, presently challengeable act by a public authority; (4) victim standing; and (5) a viable remedy notwithstanding the one-year limitation. Article 3 should not be pleaded unless the evidence describes conduct capable of meeting its exceptionally high threshold — including it without a specific evidential foundation makes the whole document look more expansive than the facts support.

## Ancillary causes of action

Unjust enrichment should not be presented, as an earlier draft did, as though continued retention of disputed land automatically refreshes a rolling six-year limitation period. A defect in title is not automatically an unjust-enrichment claim. This and any other ancillary doctrine (proprietary estoppel, for example) should sit in a holding category — potential ancillary causes of action, to be identified by counsel only if a specific unjust factor, enrichment, and at-the-expense-of relationship can actually be shown — rather than being presented as an active head of claim in the main strategy.

# Part VII — Institutional Accountability Tracks

Two corrections apply across this whole Part: first, “CADW” and “South Wales Police” are institutional labels, not necessarily the correct legal defendants; and second, continuity of an institution's name since 1988 does not by itself establish that today's body carries yesterday's liability.

| Institution (as commonly named) | Correct legal-identity question for counsel | Claim vehicle (subject to Part VI thresholds) | Status / priority |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| CADW | Cadw is understood to have no separate legal personality of its own and to sit within Welsh Government; the correct defendant is likely the Welsh Ministers (or, for the 1988 act, the Secretary of State for Wales / Welsh Office as it then was). Counsel must confirm the statutory decision-maker and any successor-liability route before pleading. | Negligence / misfeasance (subject to Part IV/VI thresholds); HRA only if the Part VI conditions are met | Most advanced evidential track — forensic critique v5.0.0 complete; legal identity of the defendant not yet confirmed |
| South Wales Police | Civil proceedings against a police force are conventionally brought against the Chief Constable of South Wales Police (or the relevant office-holder in 1988), not the force as an unincorporated body. Confirm this before any letter before claim is drafted. | Misconduct; negligence (subject to duty-of-care threshold) | Not started — high evidential value given Mary Williams' account, but defendant identity must be confirmed first |
| Vale of Glamorgan Council | The present Vale of Glamorgan Council dates from the 1996 local government reorganisation. Wales operated a two-tier county/district structure in 1988\. Counsel must identify which authority (county or district) actually exercised the relevant planning or Building Preservation Notice function in December 1988, and the statutory mechanism by which any liability or function passed to the present council. | Negligence; breach of statutory duty (subject to duty-of-care threshold) | Not started — begin the predecessor/successor analysis before any complaint or FOI is sent |
| Building Preservation Notice question | The current BPN framework (and its Welsh replacement, the Historic Environment (Wales) Act 2023\) post-dates 1988\. Before treating the absence of a BPN as a failure, identify what statutory power existed in December 1988, who held it, who could initiate it, and what role Cadw, the Welsh Office, and the local planning authority each actually had. | Feeds into the council and CADW tracks once resolved | Research gate — do not assert a BPN failure as fact until this is verified |
| Land Registry / Chief Land Registrar | Already correctly named. Second Defendant in the anchor claim. | Rectification (LRA 2002 Sch 4, subject to the possession restriction in Part V); Sch 8 indemnity if rectification causes loss | Already pleaded — no separate track needed unless a distinct registration-process failure is shown |
| Western Ground Rents Ltd (or successor) | Not automatically a contribution or third-party defendant — contribution is a mechanism between parties liable for the same damage and has its own limitation regime. WGR is better treated, for now, as a historical proprietary-chain evidence source and a possible party subject to separate corporate-existence and limitation analysis. | To be determined once corporate status is established | Not started — confirm whether WGR still exists as a legal entity before assigning it any claim vehicle |
| HMCTS / National Archives, RCAHMW, GGAT/Heneb | Evidential only — not prospective defendants. | None — archival/FOI requests only | Not started (HMCTS/NA, GGAT/Heneb); partially covered (RCAHMW) |
| Judiciary / the courts (1955 order; 1987 CA judgment) | Not a prospective defendant. | None — addressed only through the estoppel analysis in Part IV | Not a claim track |
| Central government / EU bodies | Requires precise identification of a specific department or agency and a viable cause of action before any track can start. | Uncertain — likely political rather than private law | Hold — counsel to advise on justiciability and standing |

# Part VIII — Information, Records and Preservation

Use the four routes in Part III deliberately rather than interchangeably: FOI/EIR for institutional recorded information; SAR strictly for a living family member's own personal data; archival access for historical material; and court disclosure once proceedings are genuinely live.

On preservation: an earlier draft stated that, once litigation is in contemplation, “nothing can lawfully be destroyed.” That overstates the position. The defensible formulation is that preservation notices should be issued identifying the specific material relevant to reasonably contemplated proceedings, and requesting suspension of routine disposal of potentially relevant records pending clarification of the dispute and the applicable retention obligations — not an assertion that all ordinary disposal processes become unlawful in every circumstance the moment a claim is contemplated.

# Part IX — Procedure and Pre-Action Strategy

There is no single universal pre-action sequence that applies to every institution and every cause of action. An earlier draft proposed one fixed six-step sequence (complaint → FOI → SAR → ombudsman → letter before claim → proceedings) for every party. That should be replaced with a route-specific approach, because judicial review in particular cannot safely be made to wait behind the others.

| Route | What applies |
| :---- | :---- |
| Evidence route | FOI / EIR / archive / data-protection requests, used as set out in Parts III and VIII, run at any time and not conditional on the other routes. |
| Complaint / regulatory route | Used only where the relevant mechanism (internal complaint, Public Services Ombudsman for Wales, IOPC, ICO) can produce a useful determination, or is itself a genuine prerequisite to a later step. It is a parallel accountability and evidential mechanism, not a litigation stage in its own right. |
| Private law route (negligence, misfeasance, contract, property) | Follow the relevant Civil Procedure Rules Pre-Action Protocol; send preservation and disclosure correspondence; issue a letter before claim once the position is sufficiently developed. |
| Judicial review route | Take specialist advice immediately if any live public-law decision is to be challenged. Judicial review claims must be filed promptly and in any event generally within three months of the decision — the general pre-action protocol does not extend that deadline, and this timetable must not be allowed to run behind information-gathering on other routes. |

**Two points apply to every route and should be stated prominently rather than left implicit:**

**FOI does not stop limitation running. SAR does not stop limitation running. An ombudsman or regulator complaint does not stop limitation running. A preservation letter does not stop limitation running. Only issuing a claim form (or, in judicial review, filing promptly within the applicable time limit) protects the position on the clock.**

The Public Services Ombudsman for Wales may decline to investigate where an adequate court remedy exists, and generally expects complaints within a year of the complainant becoming aware of the matter. An IOPC complaint can still be made after twelve months, but the complainant must explain the delay and there is no guarantee it will be investigated. Both are useful, genuinely independent routes to evidence and findings — neither is a limitation-preservation mechanism, and neither should be scheduled as though it were.

## Protective claim forms — a caveat, not a routine tool

Where a limitation deadline is genuinely at risk, counsel should determine whether a claim must be issued protectively, with any application for a stay pending pre-action protocol compliance made on a properly reasoned basis. This is a discretionary court process, not an entitlement, and must not be relied upon as though it automatically extends limitation or the judicial review promptness requirement.

# Part X — Costs and Sustainability

A multi-year campaign against several public bodies and a private registered proprietor is expensive in money, time, and emotional load. Treat that as a hard constraint on pace, not a line in a risk register.

* Investigate conditional fee agreements (CFAs) or damages-based agreements (DBAs), and after-the-event (ATE) insurance, before any institutional claim is issued.

* Consider protective costs orders for any claim genuinely of general public importance.

* Sequencing itself controls cost — do not run every front at once.

* Set the pace by the family's capacity to sustain the process, not only by procedural deadlines.

# Part XI — Risk Register

| Risk | Where it bites | Mitigation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1987 judgment's title-related premises are mischaracterised or overstated | Anchor claim | Use the estoppel attack map in Part IV; obtain the full 1987 bundle before drafting |
| Section 32 argument treated as a blanket proposition rather than defendant-specific | All tort claims relying on concealment | Build and evidence the concealment case separately against each defendant, per Part VI |
| HRA claim pleaded as though it converts a 1988 event into a live breach | Any HRA track | Apply the McKerr / s.7(5) analysis in Part VI before pleading; treat as a specialist conditional track |
| Duty of care or misfeasance threshold not met | CADW / council / police claims | Obtain counsel's threshold opinion before drafting; do not plead speculatively |
| Wrong legal defendant named (institutional label used instead of correct legal person) | CADW, police, council tracks | Resolve the legal-identity questions in Part VII before any letter before claim is sent |
| Judicial review promptness missed because information-gathering was allowed to run first | Any live public-law decision | Treat JR as its own route with its own three-month clock, per Part IX — never subordinate it to FOI/SAR/complaint timing |
| Missing records treated as proof of liability rather than as an evidential question | All institutional tracks | Apply the evidential chain in Part III; do not skip from absence to failure to liability |
| Costs exposure across multiple fronts | Institutional claims phase | Sequencing; protective costs orders; CFA/DBA and ATE insurance investigated early |

# Part XII — Issue-Readiness Gates

Before any claim is issued against any defendant, the following should be capable of a clear answer. This is deliberately the last substantive section: it turns the rest of this note from a campaign plan into a set of questions counsel can actually sign off against.

| Gate | Question |
| :---- | :---- |
| Title | Is there sufficient evidence that the House Plot was excluded from the relevant proprietary chain? |
| 1987 | Has counsel completed the estoppel attack map and confirmed precisely what was and was not adjudicated? |
| Standing | Are the correct persons entitled to sue identified and, if numerous, is a representation order needed? |
| Defendant | Is the correct legal person identified — not just the institutional label? |
| Possession | Who is presently in possession of the registered land, and does the Schedule 4 possession restriction apply? |
| Registration | Is Schedule 4 rectification actually the correct procedural mechanism on the facts established? |
| Limitation | What is the exact limitation period and trigger date for this specific cause of action against this specific defendant? |
| Section 32 | Is there defendant-specific evidence of deliberate concealment, tested against the Canada Square standard? |
| Public body | What exact statutory function or duty existed at the relevant historical date, and who held it? |
| Evidence | What critical missing document remains genuinely necessary before this claim can be pleaded? |
| Procedure | Is there a mandatory or relevant pre-action protocol, or a judicial review promptness clock, that governs this route? |
| Costs | Is the family realistically able to sustain this specific claim to conclusion? |

# Part XIII — Immediate Actions

| Priority | Action | Responsible | Deadline |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Identify the current registered proprietor of WA231076 from the Land Registry, and confirm who is in physical possession of the land | Solicitors | Week 1 |
| 2 | Confirm the correct legal defendant for the CADW track (Welsh Ministers / Welsh Office successor) and the police track (Chief Constable of South Wales Police) | Solicitors | Week 2 |
| 3 | Identify which local authority exercised the relevant planning/BPN function in December 1988, under the two-tier structure then in place, and how any liability passed to the present Vale of Glamorgan Council | Solicitors | Month 1 |
| 4 | Verify the December 1988 statutory framework for Building Preservation Notices before treating their absence as a failure | Solicitors / counsel | Month 1 |
| 5 | Commission the 1877 instrument search at Glamorgan Archives (D/D BUTE) and the National Archives | Solicitors / agent | Month 1 |
| 6 | Send preservation letters (in the terms set out in Part VIII, not an absolute non-destruction claim) to all prospective defendants | Solicitors | Week 1 |
| 7 | Instruct counsel for a written opinion completing the estoppel attack map (Part IV) and the Issue-Readiness Gates (Part XII) for the title claim specifically | Solicitors | Month 1 |
| 8 | Instruct counsel for a written opinion on section 32 (defendant-by-defendant) and on whether any HRA track can meet the Part VI conditions | Solicitors | Month 1 |
| 9 | Confirm whether any live public-law decision exists that triggers a judicial review promptness clock, and if so take specialist JR advice immediately, in parallel with everything else | Solicitors | Immediately |
| 10 | Investigate CFA/DBA and ATE insurance options before any institutional claim is issued | Solicitors | Month 1 |

**The decisive next step is not further drafting. It is counsel's written opinion on the Part IV estoppel analysis and the Part VI limitation position, tested against the Issue-Readiness Gates in Part XII. Everything else in this note remains provisional until that opinion is in hand.**

*This document does not constitute legal advice and should be reviewed, corrected, and adopted or discarded section by section by solicitors and counsel instructed on the full papers.*

**MASTER LEGAL & INSTITUTIONAL ACCOUNTABILITY STRATEGY**

**Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough**

*Client working note, prepared for review by instructed solicitors and counsel*

**This note is not legal advice. It is prepared for you to hand to instructed solicitors and counsel, who should treat every recommendation in it as provisional pending their own review of the full papers. No solicitor-client relationship is created by it. Limitation periods, procedural rules, and the effect of BP Properties Ltd v Buckler \[1987\] EWCA Civ 2 are complex, fact-specific matters that only a qualified solicitor can properly advise on.**

A documented, adjudicated record has value even where a monetary remedy does not follow it, and that is reflected in how the tracks below are sequenced: the title finding first, then each institution's own accountability, banked as it is obtained rather than held back for a single final result.

# Part I — Strategic Objectives

Three objectives run through the tracks below. They are not equally weighted, and the architecture in Part II exists to sequence them correctly rather than pursue all three at once.

1. Proprietary: recover the House Plot and rectify title WA231076 so the register reflects the true chain of title.

2. Institutional accountability: establish, party by party, whether CADW, the police, the local planning authority, and the private conveyancing chain (BP / WGR / predecessors) failed in duties owed to the family, and recover whatever damages or redress follows from each proven failure.

3. Documentary record: build a single, evidentially disciplined chronology (1877–2026) that has been tested in court or by a regulator, rather than asserted — the CADW critique is the working model for this, not a one-off.

The title claim is evidentially prior to almost everything else. If the House Plot was never part of the WGR/BP chain, that finding reframes the legal character of the 1988 eviction and demolition for every other claim. A civil claim against CADW or the police is stronger starting from a court finding that the family had a subsisting proprietary interest in 1988, rather than from an assertion of one.

# Part II — One Case or Many? The Architecture

UK civil procedure does not offer a single claim joining a private registered proprietor, a public heritage body, a police force, and a local authority — they sit in different courts, under different causes of action, different limitation regimes, and different standards of proof. A solicitor will resist joining them into one claim form. Equally, issuing every claim at once burns resources, creates satellite jurisdiction disputes, and lets each defendant point to the others to dilute responsibility.

The workable architecture is hub-and-spoke:

* One anchor claim (the Chancery title claim), litigated first and treated as the evidentiary hub.

* A parallel pre-action track against every other implicated party — complaints, FOI, and GDPR/SAR requests — run at the same time but not yet issued as proceedings.

* Sequential, not simultaneous, issuing of the individual institutional claims once the pre-action material against each is exhausted, any limitation deadline forces the issue, and the anchor claim's findings can be pleaded in support.

| Consideration | One combined claim | Many simultaneous claims | Hub-and-spoke |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Procedural viability | Not available — courts and defendants do not align | Available but resource-intensive | Available — correct court for each claim |
| Cost exposure | N/A | High — multiple proceedings running at once | Lower — costs staged, most claims held pre-action |
| Evidential strength | N/A | Each claim fights alone | Each spoke can rely on the hub's findings once available |
| Limitation risk | N/A | Manageable if issued together | Requires active tracking — protective claim forms may be needed even while the hub is still running |
| Pressure to settle | N/A | Diffuse — each defendant can wait out the others | Concentrated — a live FOI/complaints trail plus a live Chancery claim creates pressure without suing everyone at once |

Counsel should confirm this architecture, and in particular the limitation position for each institutional track, before any decision is taken to hold a claim pre-action rather than issue it. Some human rights and tort claims run on strict 1–6 year clocks and cannot simply wait for the title claim to conclude.

# Part III — The Anchor: The Chancery Title Claim

The draft Particulars of Claim is a workable skeleton for the hub claim. Its central discipline — not asking the court to disturb BP Properties Ltd v Buckler \[1987\], only to determine a question that judgment did not decide (whether the House Plot was ever in the WGR/BP chain at all) — is the correct posture and should not be abandoned under drafting pressure to “go further.”

## What is strong

* Confined to root-of-title, keeping it outside the adverse-possession finding actually made in 1987\.

* Pleads the family's evidence (Mary Williams' witness statement) as evidence to be tested, not as established fact, protecting the pleading from being struck out as a collateral attack.

* Puts the registered proprietor to proof of the instrument by which it says the House Plot entered its title, rather than assuming that burden.

## What is still missing before issue

* An identified First Defendant — the current registered proprietor of WA231076, named from the Land Registry entry, not left as a placeholder.

* The 1877 Bute-to-Daniel-Thomas instrument itself. Section C presently describes what the instrument is expected to say; a solicitor will want the document, or a clearly reasoned pleading of secondary evidence if it cannot be found.

* Full identification of all claimants entitled through Mary Williams' estate.

* Confirmation that the 1975 conveyance's exclusion of the farmhouse, garden and curtilage (Section H) can be shown from the instrument's own plan, not inferred.

Instruct a search of the National Archives and Glamorgan Archives (see Part V) before issuing, since disclosure obtained pre-action will strengthen Sections C, F and H. If limitation or tactics require issuing sooner, the claim can be issued on the present evidential basis and amended once the archival search concludes.

# Part IV — The Replicable Methodology: Forensic Institutional Critique

The CADW Forensic Critique is a method, not a one-off complaint, and the same method should be built for every other party before any institutional claim is issued. Three disciplines must be preserved wherever it is reapplied:

| Category | Definition | Function |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Established fact | Supported by contemporaneous documents, press, or official records | The only category that carries a positive assertion |
| Reasonable inference | Follows logically from established facts but is not itself independently confirmed | Builds pressure without overstating the evidence |
| Cannot be established | The confirming evidence is missing | Converts “we don't know” into a specific question the institution must answer — the lever that shifts the burden onto them |

## The record-lifecycle audit

For each party, request or reconstruct: file reference, title, series, opening and closure dates; the retention/disposal schedule applicable in the relevant year; destruction certificates, transfer lists, or accession records; the search methodology used (repositories, catalogues, legacy systems); and any National Archives transfer documentation. The operative question to put to every party, adapted from the CADW critique, is:

*“Show me the lawful records-management process by which your file on Great House Farm / the Williams-Buckler family ceased to exist, or produce it.”*

This does not accuse anyone of wrongdoing, so it cannot be dismissed as speculative; it is answerable only with documents, not opinion; and if the institution cannot answer it, the gap becomes evidence of a records-management failure in its own right, independent of the underlying 1988 decision.

# Part V — Party-by-Party Track Matrix

Each active track below should eventually have its own CADW-style forensic critique document. Status reflects where each currently stands.

| Party | Role in dispossession | Pre-action track | Eventual claim vehicle | Status |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| CADW | Refused emergency spot-listing Dec 1988; cannot account for record loss | FOI (in progress — ATISN 27021, further responses Jul–Aug 2026); complaint to CADW; Public Services Ombudsman for Wales if unresolved | Negligence / misfeasance in public office; HRA Art 8 / A1P1 | Forensic critique v5.0.0 complete — most advanced track |
| BP Properties Ltd (or successor registered proprietor) | Current registered proprietor of WA231076; enforced 1988 eviction and demolition | Letter before claim (Chancery); retention/preservation notice | Rectification (LRA 2002 Sch 4); proprietary declaration; possibly unjust enrichment | Anchor claim — needs Defendant identified, see Part III |
| Western Ground Rents Ltd (or successor) | 1938/1939 conveyancing predecessor in the BP chain | Corporate search to establish current legal existence/successor; disclosure request | Third-party / contribution claim if still extant; otherwise evidential only | Not yet started — confirm whether WGR still exists as a legal entity |
| Vale of Glamorgan Council (or predecessor authority) | Planning enforcement; potential Building Preservation Notice failure | FOI; council's statutory complaints procedure; Public Services Ombudsman for Wales | Negligence; breach of statutory duty; HRA Art 8 / A1P1 | Not yet started — start now, do not let it lag behind CADW |
| South Wales Police (or predecessor force) | Enforcement of 1955/1988 eviction; alleged removal of title documents by named individuals | SAR (GDPR/Data Protection Act); formal complaint; IOPC referral | Misconduct; negligence; HRA Art 3 / 8 | Not yet started — start now, high evidential value given Mary Williams' statement |
| Land Registry / Chief Land Registrar | Second Defendant in the anchor claim; registered the disputed title | Already provided for as Second Defendant; separate FOI only if a distinct registration-process failure is suspected | Rectification (LRA 2002 Sch 4); Sch 8 indemnity if rectification causes loss; negligence only if a distinct process failure is shown | Already pleaded — no separate track needed unless a distinct failure emerges |
| HMCTS / court administration / National Archives | Custodian of 1955 and 1987 court records | FOI / National Archives catalogue search; record request under court retention rules | Evidential only — not a defendant in the usual sense | Not yet started |
| RCAHMW | Held the 1974 architectural survey; unclear whether consulted by CADW | FOI; direct request confirming survey provenance and any 1988 contact with CADW | Evidential only | Partially covered in the CADW critique — needs its own direct request |
| GGAT / Heneb | 1978–80 and 1990 archaeological assessments; author of the 1989 “county treasure” description | Direct archival request | Evidential only | Not yet started — open question in the CADW critique, Part XIII.3 |
| Judiciary / the courts (1955 order; 1987 CA judgment) | Made the orders and judgment now being worked around | None — not a prospective defendant | None. Addressed only through the confined root-of-title pleading in Part III; no freestanding claim against the judiciary is proposed | Not a claim track — adjudicated background, subject to the estoppel analysis in Part III |
| Unspecified central UK government bodies / EU institutions | Alleged legislative or regulatory failure to prevent or remedy the dispossession | Not viable as currently framed — requires precise identification of a department or agency and a cause of action before any track can start | Uncertain — likely evidential or political (Senedd/Westminster petition) rather than a private-law claim; EU claims are further constrained post-Brexit and by limitation | Hold — counsel should advise on justiciability and standing before either is treated as a defendant |

Land Registry is already a Second Defendant in the anchor claim and needs no separate pre-action track unless a distinct registration failure emerges. HMCTS/National Archives, RCAHMW, and GGAT/Heneb are evidential-only — they build the record trail supporting the claims against CADW, the police, the council, and BP, and should be approached as archive requests, not adversarial correspondence. The judiciary and unspecified central government/EU bodies are not treated as defendants: the former is addressed only through the confined title pleading, and the latter should be held pending counsel's advice on justiciability rather than pursued as automatic tracks.

# Part VI — The Pre-Action Sequencing Protocol

Every institutional party — without exception — should be taken through its own complaints procedure, FOI/SAR route, and letter before claim before any claim form is issued against it. This is both fair and tactically protective: it creates a contemporaneous record of each party's position, or its failure to engage, which later supports both liability and costs arguments. The pre-action protocols in England and Wales expect this, and skipping it can cost you in costs orders even where you win. The sequence for each institutional party:

1. Internal complaint through the institution's own complaints procedure — fast, free, and creates the first documentary record of its position.

2. Freedom of Information request(s), built around the record-lifecycle audit in Part IV, addressed to the specific gaps in what that institution should hold.

3. Subject Access Request (GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018\) where personal data about named family members may be held — this can surface material an FOI exemption would otherwise block.

4. Escalation to the relevant ombudsman or regulator if the complaint is unresolved (Public Services Ombudsman for Wales for CADW/council; Independent Office for Police Conduct for the police; the Information Commissioner's Office if FOI/SAR responses are inadequate).

5. Letter before claim, once the above has produced useful disclosure or been exhausted, formally setting out the cause of action and inviting settlement or an admission before proceedings issue.

6. Proceedings, only once limitation forces the issue, or the pre-action stages have been genuinely exhausted without resolution.

Run this sequence in parallel across all institutional parties, tracking each on its own clock. CADW's is already well advanced. The police and council tracks have not started and should begin now so they do not fall dangerously behind.

# Part VII — Master Phasing Timeline

| Phase | Approx. timing | Primary activity | Governing logic |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 0 — Preservation & foundation | Now – Month 3 | Send retention/preservation letters to all prospective defendants. Commission the 1877 instrument search. Identify the current registered proprietor. Instruct leading counsel for a joint opinion on the 1987 judgment's scope. | Nothing can be lawfully destroyed once litigation is in reasonable contemplation — this precedes every other visible step |
| 1 — Anchor claim issued | Month 2 – 18 | Issue and pursue the Chancery title claim. Use disclosure obtained in it to strengthen the institutional tracks. | The title finding underwrites everything downstream |
| 2 — Pre-action institutional track | Month 0 – 24 (parallel) | Run the six-step sequence in Part VI against CADW, council, and police, and evidentially against RCAHMW/GGAT/National Archives. Issue proceedings only where limitation requires a protective claim form. | Builds the evidence base and gives every party fair opportunity to respond, without diluting resources |
| 3 — Institutional claims issued | Month 18 – 48 | Issue proceedings against whichever institutions have not settled, sequenced so the most time-pressured claims go first. | By now the anchor claim's findings, if favourable, and the pre-action disclosure are both available as evidence |
| 4 — Reparative and record phase | Month 36+ | Consolidate the adjudicated record; consider a Senedd/Westminster petition for a public inquiry under the Inquiries Act 2005; make the settled chronology public. | Accountability and record can be pursued even where limitation or estoppel has closed off a monetary remedy |

# Part VIII — Reparations Strategy

Recovery here spans several distinct heads, and counsel should value each separately rather than netting them against one another:

* Proprietary recovery: the House Plot itself, via rectification of WA231076 — the largest single asset at stake and the anchor claim's direct target.

* Civil damages: from any institution or private party found to have acted negligently, unlawfully, or in breach of statutory duty, quantified separately for each successful claim and subject to the limitation analysis in Part IX.

* Human Rights Act damages: available where an Art 8, A1P1, Art 3, or Art 6 breach is established against a public authority; typically modest, but not tied to the same limitation clock as tort claims.

* Costs recovery: where claims succeed in whole or part against public bodies, cost orders are themselves a form of accountability.

* Non-monetary outcomes: a corrected land register entry, published regulator or ombudsman findings, a court-tested chronology, and — if pursued — a Senedd or Westminster inquiry finding. These retain value even where a monetary claim fails on limitation or estoppel.

Counsel's opinion on the concealment evidence deserves particular priority: if a court accepts that documents were deliberately concealed (Mary Williams' account of the blanket-box papers being taken by Sutherland at Knapp's request), section 32 of the Limitation Act 1980 can postpone the start of the limitation clock for related claims until the concealment was, or reasonably could have been, discovered. That argument is what could reopen claims that would otherwise look time-barred, and should be tested early rather than left until the institutional claims are drafted.

# Part IX — Risk Register

| Risk | Where it bites | Mitigation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1987 CA judgment creates issue/cause of action estoppel | Anchor claim | Keep the pleading confined to root-of-title, as currently drafted; obtain the full 1987 court record before issuing |
| Limitation bars tort/HRA claims | All institutional claims | Section 32 concealment argument; protective claim forms; HRA discretion to extend |
| Institutions assert “no records” and stop there | All FOI/complaint tracks | Apply the record-lifecycle audit — demand proof of lawful disposal, not mere assertion of absence |
| Costs exposure across multiple fronts | Institutional claims phase | Sequence claims (Part VII); consider protective costs orders where claims are of general public importance; conditional fee arrangements |
| Judicial reluctance to reopen 1988 events | All institutional claims | Frame around present, ongoing consequences — unregistered title, unresolved records failure — rather than historical grievance alone |
| Sustained cost to the family across a multi-year, multi-front campaign | All phases | This is a real cost, not a legal risk lawyers manage — treat Part VII's phasing as a floor, not a target to compress |

# Part X — Immediate Next Actions

1. Identify the current registered proprietor of WA231076 from the Land Registry and name it as First Defendant.

2. Commission the 1877 Bute-to-Daniel-Thomas instrument search at Glamorgan Archives (D/D BUTE collection) before issuing, if the timeline allows.

3. Send retention/preservation letters to every prospective defendant now, before any other visible step.

4. Start the full pre-action sequence against the police and Vale of Glamorgan Council immediately, so neither track lags behind CADW's.

5. Confirm the party matrix with counsel, marking Land Registry, the judiciary, and any central government/EU bodies clearly as already-pleaded, non-justiciable, or evidential-only rather than as active tracks.

6. Ask counsel for a specific opinion on the section 32 concealment argument and on the limitation position for each institutional track, before deciding to hold any claim pre-action.

*This document does not constitute legal advice and should be reviewed, corrected, and adopted or discarded section by section by solicitors and counsel instructed on the full papers.*
